title: openai/plugins — OpenAI Plugins
content:
This repository contains a curated collection of Codex plugin examples.
Each plugin lives under plugins/<name>/ with a required
.codex-plugin/plugin.json manifest and optional companion surfaces such as
skills/, .app.json, .mcp.json, plugin-level agents/, commands/,
hooks.json, assets/, and other supporting files.
The default marketplace lives at .agents/plugins/marketplace.json and points
at the standard plugins/ directory. API key login users have a separate
marketplace at .agents/plugins/api_marketplace.json.
Highlighted richer examples in this repo include:
- plugins/figma foruse_figma , Code to Canvas, Code Connect, and design system rules
- plugins/notion for planning, research, meetings, and knowledge capture
- plugins/build-ios-apps for SwiftUI implementation, refactors, performance, and debugging
- plugins/build-macos-apps for macOS SwiftUI/AppKit workflows, build/run/debug loops, and packaging guidance
- plugins/build-web-apps for deployment, UI, payments, and database workflows
- plugins/expo for Expo and React Native apps, SDK upgrades, EAS workflows, and Codex Run actions
- plugins/netlify ,plugins/remotion , andplugins/google-slides for additional public skill- and MCP-backed plugin bundles

report.summary: OpenAI's openai/plugins repo collects curated Codex plugin examples, defining a manifest-plus-skills/MCP structure and marketplaces to standardize how agents gain new capabilities.
report.background: AI coding agents moved from autocomplete to autonomous tool-using systems in 2025, and the missing piece became distribution: how do you package, discover and install new agent abilities? Anthropic pushed 'skills' and MCP (Model Context Protocol) as a connective standard; Cursor, GitHub Copilot and others built their own extension formats. OpenAI's Codex, relaunched as an agentic coding product, now answers with a plugin spec: a required .codex-plugin/plugin.json manifest plus optional skills/, .app.json, .mcp.json, agents/, commands/, hooks.json and assets/ surfaces. The repo doubles as a showcase, bundling first- and third-party integrations from Figma, Notion, Expo, Netlify, Remotion and Google Slides, plus vertical examples for iOS, macOS and web app building. It effectively turns Codex into a platform rather than just a model.
key_points: A standard plugin layout: every plugin lives under plugins/<name>/ and must ship a .codex-plugin/plugin.json manifest, with optional companion surfaces for skills, MCP servers, sub-agents, slash commands, hooks, app metadata and assets. This gives third-party tools one predictable packaging format instead of ad-hoc prompt folders.

Two marketplaces ship in the repo: .agents/plugins/marketplace.json is the default catalog pointing at the plugins/ directory, while API-key login users get a separate .agents/plugins/api_marketplace.json. That split hints at distinct distribution or entitlement channels for subscription versus API customers.

The highlighted examples are notably practical: Figma for Code to Canvas, Code Connect and design-system rules; Notion for planning, research and meetings; build-ios-apps and build-macos-apps for SwiftUI/AppKit workflows; build-web-apps for deployment, UI, payments and databases; and Expo for React Native plus EAS and Codex Run actions.

Several bundles are explicitly skill- and MCP-backed, meaning they combine prompt-level 'skills' with MCP servers for real tool access. Plugins such as Netlify, Remotion and Google Slides show the pattern works across hosting, video generation and office productivity, not just coding.

For developers, the repo is a working reference implementation: copy a plugin folder, mirror the manifest and surface files, and publish your own integration. That lowers the barrier from 'write a custom agent' to 'wrap an existing API or workflow as a plugin.'
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is OpenAI trying to make its plugin manifest and marketplace an expected shape for agent extensibility, alongside MCP and Anthropic's skills. If Codex plugins gain traction, competing agents face pressure to support or translate the format. For developers, it means reference code, less boilerplate and a distribution channel where a single manifest can expose skills, tools, commands and sub-agents to millions of users. For regular users, Codex becomes more useful inside Figma, Notion, Expo and Netlify without leaving the agent, though the subscription-versus-API marketplace split could complicate discovery and billing. The larger risk is fragmentation: three or four competing plugin standards and no clear winner yet.
report.tools: Watch the Model Context Protocol (MCP) spec and community server lists, since many of these plugins wrap MCP servers. Anthropic's Claude Skills and Claude Code plugins are the closest competing standard; Cursor rules and GitHub Copilot extensions show other models. On the open-source side, Cline, Continue.dev, Aider and OpenHands are worth studying for how they package tools and prompts. Directly try the repo's Figma, Notion, Expo, Netlify, Remotion and Google Slides examples as templates.
